**Gannon, J Andrés. "A Text-as-Data Approach to Measuring Interstate Relations Using National Security Strategies." Working paper.**

[Abstract]{.underline}: How states regard one another -- which states command attention, and with what evaluative orientation -- is central to international relations, yet it is measured with proxies that are largely binary, symmetric, and slow-moving because they are built for other purposes. I develop and validate a text-as-data method that recovers directed dyad-year indices of a state's expressed salience (prominence) and affinity (evaluative stance) toward other states from its national security strategy. The method automates the judgments a careful reader would make -- which states a government names, how prominently, and in what evaluative terms -- and makes them consistently across hundreds of documents. Applied to a new public corpus of 438 national security strategy documents issued by 92 countries (1962–2024) -- to date the most comprehensive cross-national, multi-decade collection of security-strategy texts -- the approach produces continuous, directional, and time-varying measures of interstate posture. Because governments revise these documents every few years rather than every few decades, the measures register shifts in stated posture as they happen, an early signal alongside slower-moving indicators such as UN votes and alliances. The measures converge with benchmarks such as alliance portfolio similarity and UN voting patterns where they should, track human judgments of expressed orientation, and diverge from the benchmarks where expressed and behavioral alignment part ways. In application, the scores add incremental predictive validity for militarized interstate dispute onset and diplomatic visits beyond these benchmarks, and reveal an asymmetry -- cooperation tracks both a target's prominence and its warmth, while conflict tracks prominence most strongly, with expressed hostility contributing a smaller association. The corpus, processing code, and derived measures are publicly released, providing a replicable tool for extracting conveyed relationships from political texts.
